title: runs on an algorithm built for a robot.
description:
runs on an algorithm built for a robot. A* is the standard for pathfinding in games and maps. It was written in 1968 to help one machine cross a cluttered room without walking into things.

At Stanford Research Institute, plotting routes for Shakey, a robot so unsteady that the team named it for the way it rattled and shook whenever it moved.

The star arrived with a proof. Raphael refined it; Hart showed that, given an honest guess of the distance left, it always finds the shortest path. A* meant: we can prove this one is optimal.

It isn't. Even a co-author first guessed it came from Kleene-star syntax. Hart says no: it's the statistician's star for an optimal value. The real meaning went unrecorded for fifty years.

Gaming's smartest navigator is named after a robot that couldn't hold still.

Sources:
- https://cacm.acm.org/opinion/a-search/: Communications of the ACM viewpoint, read directly: A* was published in 1968 by Hart, Nilsson and Raphael; the authors themselves recount that Nilsson devised it to plan Shakey the Robot's route through a room of obstacles and first called it 'Algorithm A'; Raphael improved it and Hart proved it optimal given an admissible heuristic, so they named it A* 'to distinguish it from any simpler algorithm A'; Hart says the star denotes an optimal value (from statistics) and 'has nothing whatsoever to do with Kleene star syntax', while co-author Nilsson initially guessed the Kleene interpretation; the meaning had gone undocumented until this piece.
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shakey_the_robot: Wikipedia, read directly: Shakey was developed ~1966-1972 at the AI Center of Stanford Research Institute (SRI); A* was one of its notable results; the name came from its tall build and 'tendency to shake', quoted: 'it shakes like hell and moves around, let's just call it Shakey.'
